title: What is Salmonella and what can you do to avoid catching it?

content.content: Salmonella is the group of bacteria behind one of the most common types of food poisoning in the UK, and while for most people it means a few unpleasant days at home, for others it can lead to serious illness. With UKHSA currently helping to investigate a national outbreak that may be linked to eggs imported from outside of the UK, we've answered some of the questions we're most commonly asked about this bacteria, the symptoms it causes, and how we track it.
What is Salmonella?
There are more than 2,500 different types of Salmonella. These bacteria live naturally in the guts of many domestic and wild animals, including chickens, cattle, pigs, hedgehogs, snakes and lizards.
The type most commonly responsible for making people ill in England is Salmonella Enteritidis.
Infection with Salmonella is known as salmonellosis.
How do you catch Salmonella?

Most people become infected through eating contaminated food. Salmonella can be found in foods such as eggs, chicken, pork and dairy products. Fruit and vegetables can also carry the bacteria if they've been in contact with livestock, manure or untreated water.
It is possible in rare cases to catch Salmonella from close contact with someone who has diarrhoea, or from contact with an unwell animal.

Good hygiene is vital. Wash your hands thoroughly after using the toilet and before preparing or handling food, wash utensils and chopping boards with hot water and cook food thoroughly. If you have symptoms yourself, avoid preparing food for others where you can.
What are the symptoms?
Symptoms typically include diarrhoea, stomach cramps and sometimes vomiting and fever. These usually appear between 12 and 72 hours after infection, and illness typically lasts 4 to 7 days.

For most people, Salmonella causes a bout of gastroenteritis that clears up on its own. However, some people are at greater risk of more severe illness, including bloodstream infections, sepsis and, in rare cases, multi-organ failure.
How should it be treated?
Most people can manage Salmonella infection without needing to see a doctor.
The key things to do are:

There are also some things to avoid. Don't drink fruit juice or fizzy drinks, as these can make diarrhoea worse. Don't dilute baby formula, and don't give children under 12 medicines to stop diarrhoea, or give aspirin to children under 16.
A pharmacist can help if you or your child show signs of dehydration, are in a higher-risk group, or need something to stop diarrhoea for a few hours. They may suggest oral rehydration sachets.

You should call NHS 111 if you or your child has signs of dehydration that don't improve with rehydration sachets, can't keep fluids down, have bloody diarrhoea, or have diarrhoea that is not reducing in 3 days. If you're worried about a baby under 12 months, or a child under 5 shows signs of dehydration, call 111.
Call 999 or go to A&E for more serious symptoms, such as vomiting blood, a sudden severe headache or tummy ache, breathing difficulties, confusion, or blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin.
Is anyone more at risk, and what should they do differently?

While Salmonella causes a short, unpleasant illness for most people, some groups are more vulnerable to severe disease. This includes older people, pregnant women, young children and anyone with a weakened immune system such as those with cancer, kidney or liver failure, uncontrolled diabetes, steroid treatment or chemotherapy.

If you're in one of these groups, it's worth taking extra care, particularly around eggs. Eggs remain a healthy and safe part of the diet when properly handled and cooked, and you don't need to stop eating them. Ensure you use eggs with the British Lion mark or marked ‘Laid in Britain’. If you're eating out or buying food containing eggs that may not be British, it's safest to make sure any eggs you eat are thoroughly cooked. This means avoiding dishes such as soft boiled or poached eggs, fresh mayonnaise, mousses, soufflés and hollandaise sauce, unless you know the eggs used meet these assurance standards.
If you're in a vulnerable group and develop symptoms of Salmonella, it's worth seeking medical advice promptly rather than waiting to see if things improve on their own.
What does UKHSA do to monitor Salmonella and other gastro infections?
UKHSA's Gastrointestinal Infections, Food Safety and One Health (GIFSOH) division is responsible for monitoring cases of Salmonella and other gastrointestinal infections across the country.
This monitoring relies heavily on whole genome sequencing (WGS), a laboratory technique that allows scientists to compare the genetic fingerprint of bacteria from different cases.

When an unusual increase in cases is detected, UKHSA launches an outbreak investigation. This involves working closely with public health and food safety agencies across the UK and devolved administrations, as well as the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA) and the Food Standards Agency (FSA). Investigators interview affected people to gather information about their symptoms and possible sources of infection, helping to build a picture of where contamination may have occurred and what control measures are needed.
Where can I find more information?
You can find wider UKHSA data on Salmonella on our website.

title: Services Week 2026 Wrap Up
authors: Steph Rowe, GDS Senior Events Manager

content.content: Thank you to everyone who made Services Week 2026 such a resounding success! It was inspiring to see the community come together to share, learn, and collaborate on improving public services.
This year, we saw an incredible turnout with around 4,000 attendees across 80 sessions, delivered by community members from over 30 different government departments.

Our most popular sessions included a talk from Lou Downe on "Bad services: how to fix services that don’t work", the User-Centred Design (UCD) team at Ofgem gave a popular demonstration on "Practical AI for User-Centred Design: Lessons from Experimenting with AI", and the Government Digital Service delivered an engaging session on "The Future of the Digital Service Standard".
Attendees from across the community told us that Services Week has helped them learn about other services, build connections and share practical approaches to service design.
They loved getting a clearer picture of different service areas and seeing how other teams put design principles into practice.
We are looking forward to hosting the event again next year with even more sessions to explore. We hope to be joined by many of you again, as well as lots of new faces.

We look forward to carrying this momentum forward, using the connections and collaborative spirit fostered over this week to continue supporting one another as we build and refine our community throughout the year ahead.
Join the Conversation

The energy doesn't have to end with Services Week! We encourage you to join the Services Week community on Slack using your government email address. It's the best place to stay connected with the service design community, share news, and ask questions.
Introducing "A Problem Shared"

To keep the collaborative spirit alive, we are launching a new monthly initiative called 'A Problem Shared' on our government wide Slack channel. Each month, we'll feature a specific service design challenge or dilemma from a government team and invite you to share your thoughts, advice, and lessons learned.
This month’s question is:
Whether you have practical examples, lessons learned, useful resources, or simply a perspective to share, we'd love to hear from you.

Do you have a tricky problem or a service design question you'd like the community's help with? Post your question directly on the Slack channel, or get in touch with the GDS events team to submit your challenge for a future discussion.
We look forward to the conversations this will spark and thank you for your continued commitment to building such a strong, collaborative community.

description: This year's Services Week saw an incredible 4,000 attendees across 80 sessions, delivered by over 30 different government departments. We reflect on the event's success and how to stay connected to the community.

title: Two Years On: My Reflections as Chief Regulator

content.content: Two years ago, the Environment Agency created the Chief Regulator's Group to provide strategic leadership for regulation. We’re helping create a more consistent, effective and proportionate regulatory system and strengthening the connection between strategy, policy and delivery.

Since then, my team and I have been driving that transformation. Meaningful change can take time. But we have made good strides forward as we move from improving individual parts of regulation towards creating a more joined-up and consistent regulatory system.
Improving transparency and access

For the first time, the public can read Compliance Assessment Report (CAR) forms without raising an information request. We've now shared thousands of water quality, waste, installations, and intensive pig and poultry forms on the Public Register Online.

At the same time, improved training and assurance have raised the quality of information available to the public on permit holder performance. We're building on this momentum, with more sectors to follow.
Faster, smarter permitting

Permitting is at the centre of our improvement work, and the Accelerated Permitting Transformation Programme is already delivering results. Queue times are at a three-year low, and the backlog has been reduced by over three-quarters. Enhanced validation has also cut determination times for complex applications by up to 100 days.

We’ve also introduced a Priority Tracked Service for complex multi-permit and Nationally Significant Infrastructure (NSIP) sites, currently supporting over 60 developments in housing, energy, infrastructure, mining and technology with strong customer feedback.

Our Regulatory Services Programme is powering our digital transformation by delivering smarter online journeys for our customers. Several types of permit applications are now fully digital, including Paper, Cardboard, and Plastic (PCP), Healthcare Waste (HCW), Waste Mattresses (WM), and Materials Recycling Facilities (MRF). Alongside this, an expansion of GOV.UK Pay for permit applications under £5,000 has saved a significant amount of processing time.
Driving forward sector improvements
We support responsible businesses to thrive sustainably while acting firmly when standards fall short.

Two priority areas have been water quality and waste crime. In March, we published our 10-point plan on waste crime to strengthen and accelerate action in this growing area of concern. It focuses on earlier intervention and stronger enforcement against poor performers, while tightening controls and accountability across the waste supply chain.

For the first time, our water regulation teams completed more than 10,000 inspections of water company assets in a single year, identifying permit breaches in 22% of cases. This has built a clear, evidence-based picture of non-compliance which will shape our future regulation.

By equipping our regulatory teams with better tools, we are enabling them to make stronger use of data and insights. One example is a new digital system that will make it easier for our officers to record, track and manage noncompliance, improving follow up on actions from previous inspections. This Regulatory Compliance Service (RCS) is already in use across our Water Quality inspections and will soon roll out to other sectors including waste.
Across all sectors, we are also developing new regulation plans that focus on the real-world outcomes we want our regulation to achieve.

We are striving to provide clear, proportionate and predictable regulation. That means reducing uncertainty and enabling investment by stepping back where risks are low, taking an evidence-based approach where they’re higher, and acting firmly when needed. For example, in waste, we are setting new minimum inspection frequencies for different types of sites, focusing our effort on poor performers and high‑risk sites whilst reducing routine regulatory activity at consistently well performing sites.
Strengthening our regulatory profession

Whilst we are accelerating our use of digital, data and AI, I firmly believe that people remain at the heart of good regulation. That’s why we are strengthening regulation across the Environment Agency by establishing a Regulation Profession and investing in the learning, development and infrastructure needed to support them.

Through accredited training and new pathways with industry and academia, we are building a confident, skilled workforce supported by cutting-edge digital tools. In the waste sector for example, we are using AI and machine learning to strengthen compliance analytics, detect waste related risks and optimise assessments.
New approaches to drive progress

New approaches are key to driving progress. We’ve recently taken up the Lead Environmental Regulator position on four pilot projects – East West Rail, Lighthouse Green Fuels, Sizewell C and the Trelavour Lithium Project. This is providing developers with clearer, earlier, and more coordinated environmental guidance across environmental regulators, while maintaining robust protections.

We are also supporting innovation in areas like decarbonisation. Notable regulatory milestones include issuing the first UK refinery carbon capture and storage (CCS) permit and securing the VPI Immingham carbon capture permit - both enabling significant industrial decarbonisation.
Through our commitment to proportionate regulation and delivering environmental outcomes, we’re taking firm action where risks are high while exploring opportunities to step back where risks are low.

The Earned Autonomy programme is one example. We're working with trusted partners such as the Rivers Trust, National Trust and Forestry Commission to deliver nature recovery projects faster and more efficiently, while developing new standard rule permits, increasing exemptions, and working towards a Nature Recovery Regulatory Position Statement. A recent Regulatory Position Statement (RPS) for low-risk abstraction for nature recovery actions and fish or eel passage builds on an earlier low-risk impounding works RPS, allowing a more proportionate, risk-based approach that removes unnecessary barriers to habitat restoration, nature recovery and natural flood management projects.
Looking ahead

Our ambition is a regulatory system that is digitally enabled, risk-driven, transparent and easier to navigate. By combining better data, stronger regulatory capability and smarter technology, we can target our efforts where they achieve the greatest environmental outcomes while providing greater certainty for those we regulate.

While our transformation is by no means complete, action is underway. We have a clear understanding of what needs to be done. Independent reviews by important bodies such as the Office for Environmental Protection and the National Audit Office, alongside recommendations from Dan Corry and John Fingleton, continue to act as catalysts for change.

Lasting change cannot be delivered by the Environment Agency alone. It depends on Government setting new policies and reforming legislation and on those we regulate working with us towards a shared ambition of better environmental outcomes.

There is far more happening than I can cover in one blog. In the coming months, I will publish my next Chief Regulator report, providing a detailed overview of progress against our EA2030 strategy and the vision I outlined in my previous report.
Please follow the Chief Regulator’s LinkedIn page for further updates.

title: Forests for water: applying the UK Forestry Standard in practice

content.content: In this blog, I will cover the practical steps forest managers can take to manage their water environment. These steps include maintaining buffer zones, minimising soil disturbance and the careful timing of forest operations to protect watercourses and downstream communities. When forests are properly managed, they can protect water systems, especially with climate change intensifying flood and drought risks.
Water catchment management
Water is a fundamental natural resource that underpins ecosystems, agriculture and industry. Trees, woodlands and forests influence how water is captured, stored and released.

When rain falls on a woodland, trees intercept much of it before it ever reaches the soil. What does reach the ground tends to soak in rather than run off the surface, partly because tree roots loosen the soil and create channels for water to penetrate. Tree roots also anchor the soil and reduce erosion. From there, water makes its way back to the atmosphere through evapotranspiration, which is the combined process of evaporation from the soil surface and the moisture plants draw up and release through their leaves.

As a result, woodland creation and management play an important role in determining both water quantity and water quality across an entire catchment (the area of land where all surface water collects and drains to a single outlet).

The UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) places safeguarding the water environment at the heart of sustainable forest management. It recognises forest systems as integral parts of integrated catchment management, where land use must balance environmental protection with social and economic objectives.

Well planned and managed forests can protect water resources and support freshwater ecosystems, provided forestry operations are designed to avoid adverse impacts on hydrology and sensitive water environments.
Water protection benefits

Species-rich, diverse forests can provide strong protection for water resources when designed and managed appropriately. Permanent vegetation cover, limited soil disturbance and relatively low chemical inputs mean that woodland generally poses a lower risk to water quality than many alternative land uses. Trees help stabilise soils, reduce erosion, intercepting nutrients and pollutants before they reach watercourses.

The UKFS requires forestry operations to protect both surface water and groundwater, reflecting legal obligations and good practice. Buffer areas alongside watercourses are a key measure, reducing sediment delivery, pesticide drift and nutrient runoff. These buffers also protect riverbanks and allow riparian habitats (the interface between land and a watercourse) to develop, delivering wider ecological benefits.
Flood risk management

Flooding is an increasing risk across the UK, driven by climate change and land‑use pressures. Forests can contribute to flood risk management by intercepting rainfall, increasing infiltration and slowing the movement of water through catchments. Woodland soils with good structure and organic matter can store significant volumes of water, reducing rapid runoff during heavy rainfall.

The UKFS supports the use of woodland as part of a natural flood management approach, particularly where planting is targeted in areas upstream of communities at risk. However, it also highlights that poorly planned and managed forestry can increase flood risk.

Inappropriate drainage, road construction or large‑scale harvesting can accelerate runoff and sediment delivery to rivers. Forest design and operational planning must therefore ensure that woodland management does not increase flood risk to downstream communities or infrastructure.
Freshwater ecology

Forests influence freshwater ecosystems through their effects on shading, water temperature, sediment inputs and organic material. Riparian woodland is recognised by the UKFS as a priority habitat that supports diverse plant and animal communities, providing important ecological connectivity along rivers and streams.

The UKFS requires forest managers to identify and protect freshwater habitats, including streams, rivers, wetlands and spawning areas essential for the reproduction and development of aquatic wildlife. Small watercourses, even those less than one metre wide, are recognised as ecologically important and must be protected from compaction, sedimentation and pollution.
Appropriate buffer zone management, native species planting and careful timing of forest operations will all help safeguard freshwater ecology while supporting wider woodland objectives.
Planting near water bodies

Planning forestry operations near water bodies requires you to think at a catchment scale – considering not just the land in front of you, but how your activities could affect water further downstream.

The UKFS requires woodland creation and management proposals to consider downstream water supplies, designated conservation sites and water‑dependent habitats. Where activities may affect water quantity or quality, you should engage early with relevant authorities.

In England, if you are planning to plant within 8 metres of a main river, 16 metres of a tidal estuary where there are flood defences, or within Flood Zones 2 or 3, you may be required to assess the flood risks of your activity and get a permit from the Environment Agency.

Minimum buffer widths are set out by the UKFS to protect watercourses, lakes and reservoirs, with wider buffers applied where sites are particularly sensitive, slopes are steep or water supplies are present. Forest drainage systems must discharge before buffer areas and never directly into water bodies. Infrastructure such as bridges and culverts must be designed to avoid erosion, bank instability and barriers to fish movement.
Climate change implications

Climate change is placing growing pressure on the water environment, bringing more intense rainfall, higher flood risk, longer dry periods and rising waterbody temperatures. The UKFS integrates climate change adaptation into woodland planning, requiring forest managers to ensure their woodlands are resilient to both wetter and drier conditions, and to pick species that are appropriate to future climate conditions.

Woodlands can help moderate extreme water flows, stabilise soils and provide shade, helping to regulate water temperatures to benefit aquatic species. At the same time, forest infrastructure and drainage systems must be designed to cope with projected changes in rainfall intensity and volume. Planning for climate change is therefore a core element of sustainable forest management under the UKFS.
Water quality management

Protecting water quality is both a legal requirement and a central principle of the UKFS. Forestry operations must not allow polluting substances to enter controlled waters, including streams, rivers, lakes and groundwater. You must carefully manage use of pesticides, fertilisers, fuels and oils if your forest is to be managed sustainably.

You should minimise chemical use and make sure any applications are planned carefully to avoid runoff and leaching into watercourses. Keep storage and refuelling areas locked, well away from watercourses and have a plan in case of spillages or pollution incidents. These measures help protect drinking water supplies, aquatic habitats and public confidence in sustainable forestry.
Operational guidelines

Effective water protection depends on translating principles into day‑to‑day practice. Before work begins, your forest management and operational plans should identify water features, sensitive soils and drainage pathways. Use maps and site assessments to guide contractors and managers during operations.
Key principles to follow include:
Special considerations for water

Some locations require additional safeguards under the UKFS. These include drinking water catchments, designated conservation sites and areas supporting sensitive freshwater species such as freshwater pearl mussels and Atlantic salmon. In such cases, you will need wider buffers, stricter controls on operations and you may require closer liaison with regulators.

Riparian zones are also key pathways for invasive non‑native species such as Himalayan balsam and American skunk cabbage. These can spread and require coordinated control to protect watercourses and native habitats.

Where forestry interacts with floodplains, consider opportunities to restore riparian and wet woodland, reconnect rivers to floodplains and enhance natural water storage, subject to regulatory requirements.

description: Chris Waterfield, Carbon and Water Woodland Advisor, explains how you can apply UK Forestry Standards to create and manage woodlands to improve flood alleviation, water quality and aquatic habitats.
